Compare the version where Elena's first sentence is "How did that happen?" — a fair question, asked at the wrong second. Nadia explains defensively, Marcus never mentions his near-miss, Priya says nothing about the contact list, and the folder problem survives to catch the next new joiner. The content of the meeting is identical. What differs is which sentence came first.

docs.title: 6. Where it breaks
docs.text:
• Safety for some. Climate is often uneven along lines of tenure, seniority, language, or being the only person like themselves in the room. An average score can hide a person sitting at 1. Read the spread.
  • Confusing safety with consensus. You still make calls people dislike. Safety means they can say so first, and that you say plainly it was your call and why — not that the call changes.
  • Performance masquerading as safety. Someone repeatedly missing agreed commitments is not a safety issue and should not be handled as one. That is Module 6.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Run the seven-statement check in section 2 with your team this month, anonymously, including the free-text question. Before you read the results, write down your predicted average for each item — the gap between your prediction and the result is the more useful number.

Then do the harder half. Recall the last three times someone brought you bad news. Write down your literal first sentence each time, as best you remember it, and compare it against the table in section 3. If your first sentence was a question about cause rather than a thank-you, rehearse the replacement out loud now, so that it's available when you next need it under pressure.

docs.title: 04 · Team Development Stages (Tuckman's Model)
docs.text: A team that argued productively for six weeks and then settled into smooth delivery did not get lucky, and a team that has been polite for nine months is not necessarily healthy. Groups move through a fairly predictable sequence, and the leadership behaviour that works at one stage actively harms the next one. The most common error at this level is treating storming as a discipline problem and suppressing it — which produces a team that is permanently stuck in a courteous, low-trust forming state. This module gives you a stage diagnostic, a behaviour-per-stage table you can act from tomorrow, and a worked example of moving a stuck team through storming on purpose.

docs.title: 1. The five stages
docs.text:
Tuckman's model, with the fifth stage — added later, and the one most leaders skip entirely.

Stage What it sounds like What the team needs from you Forming Polite, cautious, questions directed at you, everyone agrees Direction. Clear goals, who does what, low ambiguity Storming Disagreement about approach, ownership and standards; some of it personal Facilitation. Surface the conflict, hold the norms, don't pick sides early Norming "How we do things here" emerges; people cover for each other Participation. Hand over decisions, codify the norms, resist re-centralising Performing High autonomy, healthy disagreement, you hear about problems after they're solved Delegation. Supply context, remove obstacles, get out of the way Adjourning Project ends, people move on; usually unacknowledged Closure. Name what was built, capture the learning, help people land

Two things that matter more than the diagram does. First, the sequence is not one-way: a new joiner, a reorg, a new manager, or a change of goal will drop a performing team straight back to forming, and that drop is normal rather than a failure. Second, storming is not optional. A team that never storms has not skipped a stage; it has buried one, and the disagreements are happening in DMs instead.

docs.title: 2. A stage diagnostic
docs.text:
Answer these honestly, then read the pattern rather than a total.

TEAM STAGE DIAGNOSTIC

A. Where do questions go?
   ( ) Almost all to me                                    -> Forming
   ( ) To me, but as appeals against each other            -> Storming
   ( ) To each other, escalating to me by exception        -> Norming
   ( ) To each other; I hear the summary                   -> Performing

B. What happens when two people disagree in a meeting?
   ( ) It doesn't happen                                   -> Forming
   ( ) It gets tense, or moves offline and festers         -> Storming
   ( ) They work it out, sometimes needing a nudge         -> Norming
   ( ) They resolve it and nobody reports it as an event   -> Performing

C. How do people describe the team's way of working?
   ( ) They describe my instructions                       -> Forming
   ( ) Differently from each other, with irritation        -> Storming
   ( ) Consistently, in their own words                    -> Norming
   ( ) Consistently, and they've changed it since I set it -> Performing

D. When something goes wrong, when do I find out?
   ( ) Immediately — nobody will act without me            -> Forming
   ( ) Late, and framed as someone else's fault            -> Storming
   ( ) Promptly, framed as a problem to solve              -> Norming
   ( ) After it's handled, as information                  -> Performing

E. What happens if I'm away for two weeks?
   ( ) Work stalls                                         -> Forming
   ( ) Open disputes stall it                              -> Storming
   ( ) It runs, with some decisions held for me            -> Norming
   ( ) It runs                                             -> Performing

Mostly one letter -> that stage.
Split between two adjacent stages -> you are in transition; lead
   for the earlier one.
Split between non-adjacent stages (e.g. Forming and Performing) ->
   you probably have two sub-teams, not one team. Diagnose separately.

docs.title: 3. The stage-appropriate behaviour table
docs.text:
The failure is almost always a mismatch: right behaviour, wrong stage.

Stage Do this Stop doing this Classic mistake Forming Set explicit goals, roles and decision rights; run structured meetings Asking "what do you all think?" into silence Mistaking politeness for alignment and declaring the team high-performing Storming Name the conflict as expected; run the Module 2 structures; enforce behaviour norms hard and opinion norms not at all Taking sides; going quiet and hoping Reading disagreement as insubordination and suppressing it Norming Get the norms written down by them; delegate a real decision; publicly back one you'd have made differently Re-opening settled decisions Re-centralising the moment quality dips once Performing Supply context and air cover; ask what's in the way; absorb organisational noise Attending meetings that don't need you Boredom-driven meddling — inventing a reorg because you feel underused Adjourning Hold a proper close: what was built, what was learned, what each person can now do that they couldn't Letting it dissolve silently Rolling straight into the next thing, so nobody's growth gets named

docs.title: 4. A worked example: entering storming deliberately
docs.text:
Owen has led a five-person internal communications team for four months, after a merger brought two smaller teams together. Everyone is pleasant, everyone defers, every decision comes to him. He runs the diagnostic and scores Forming on all five questions — at month four, which is the warning sign. The two legacy teams hold incompatible working assumptions that nobody has said aloud. He decides to surface the conflict on purpose, in a working session.

Owen: I want to name something. We've been together four months and I don't think we've had a single real disagreement in this room. That's not because we agree — it's because we haven't said what we think. That's normal at this point, and I'd like to get past it today.

Owen: So, a specific question, and I want the actual answer. When a business unit asks us for a comms plan with four days' notice, what should we do?

(Silence.)

Owen: I'll make it easier. Jules, what did your old team do?

Jules: We said yes. Always. If comms says no, they go around us and send something worse.

Owen: Ravi, what did yours do?

Ravi: We said no. We had a two-week intake rule and we held it, because otherwise you spend the whole year on other people's fire drills and the planned work never happens.

Jules: And what happened when you said no?

Ravi: Sometimes they escalated. Mostly they planned better the next time.

Jules: That would never have flown with our directors.

Owen: Good — that's the disagreement, and it's a real one. I'm not resolving it by decree. Two rules for the next twenty minutes: argue about the approach, not about which old team was better run; and before you rebut, say back what the other person's reason is.

Ravi: Jules's reason is that a hard no doesn't stop the comms going out, it just makes it happen without us — which is worse than a rushed plan.

Jules: And Ravi's is that if we never protect the calendar, the planned work is the thing that dies, every time.

Owen: Both true. What's a rule that respects both?

Sofia: Tiering. Anything that goes to more than 200 people or is externally visible needs the two-week intake. Below that, we take it in and do a cut-down version.

Ravi: I could live with that if "cut-down" is actually defined, so it isn't just a full plan under time pressure.

Jules: Then let's define it. Three assets, no bespoke design, no review cycle beyond the requester.

Owen: Write those two things down as ours, not mine, and put them on the team page by Friday. I'll back it when someone escalates — and someone will, in about three weeks.

That session was uncomfortable, and that was the point. Owen supplied the permission, the norms and the reflect-back rule; the team supplied all of the content. Within a month the diagnostic moved to Norming on questions A, B and C. Note his last line: at the norming stage the leader's job is to publicly hold a boundary the team set, especially the first time it is tested. One failure to back it returns the team to forming immediately.

docs.title: 5. Regression is not failure
docs.text: When a team drops back a stage, say so out loud. "We've added two people and changed the goal, so we're going to feel like a new team for about a month — I'll be more directive for a bit, and that's temporary" converts a confusing experience into an expected one. Teams tolerate regression well when it is named, and badly when it is denied.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Run the diagnostic in section 2 for your team this week, then run it separately for two or three individuals — people join at their own pace, and a new starter is in forming even when the team is performing.

Now take your result to the table in section 3 and find your own mismatch: name one thing from the "stop doing this" column for your current stage that you actually did in the last two weeks. Replace it with one specific action from the "do this" column, on a date. If you scored Forming past the three-month mark, make that the exercise instead — plan a session like Owen's, built around one real question on which you know two people quietly disagree.

docs.title: 05 · Delegation Deep Dive
docs.text: Level 1 covered handing over a task. This module covers the two things that actually limit a leader's capacity: handing over a decision, and refusing to absorb conflict that belongs to someone else. Most managers who believe they delegate well are delegating execution and retaining judgement — the report does the work, you approve the outcome, and your calendar stays full while nobody grows past the approval step. The symptom is a manager who cannot take two consecutive weeks off. This module gives you a seven-level delegation scale, a written delegation contract, a rule for handling escalated conflict, and two worked examples.

docs.title: 1. Seven levels of delegation
docs.text:
"Delegate more" is useless advice because delegation is not binary. Naming the level converts a vague handover into a shared expectation.

Level Who decides You say 1 · Tell You decide, they execute "Here's the decision and why." 2 · Sell You decide, and you sell it "Here's the decision; let me explain the reasoning so you can carry it." 3 · Consult You decide, after their input "I want your view before I decide. The call is mine." 4 · Agree You decide together "Neither of us decides alone; we land it jointly." 5 · Advise They decide, with your input "My view is X. It's your call, and I'll back whichever way you go." 6 · Inquire They decide, then tell you "You decide. Tell me what you chose and why, afterwards." 7 · Delegate They decide; you don't need to know "It's yours. I don't need to be in it at all."

Three rules that make this usable:

  • State the level out loud, at the start. The single most common delegation failure is a level mismatch: you thought level 6, they thought level 3, so they wait for you and you think they're passive.
  • Level per decision, not per person. A report can be at 7 on supplier scheduling and 3 on anything touching a regulator, at the same time, and that is coherent rather than inconsistent.
  • Move one level at a time, and say when. "You're at 5 on this now; after the next two, I want you at 6" turns delegation into a visible development path instead of an unpredictable weather system.

docs.title: 2. The delegation contract
docs.text:
For anything meaningful, five minutes writing this down prevents weeks of drift. Fill it in with the person, not for them.

DELEGATION CONTRACT
Decision or area: ______________________  Owner: ______________
Level (1-7): ____   Review date: __________

OUTCOME
  What good looks like (in observable terms):
  What is explicitly NOT in scope:

CONSTRAINTS  (the real boundaries — be exhaustive, they can't guess)
  Budget ceiling:
  People who must be consulted:
  Deadlines that are immovable:
  Decisions that must come back to me, and why:

INFORMATION
  What I know that they don't (context, history, politics):
  Who has the rest of it:

AUTHORITY
  What they can commit on my behalf:
  How they should describe their mandate to others:
  What I will say publicly to back that mandate:

CHECK-INS
  Cadence:                        Format:
  What I will do at a check-in:  (review progress / answer questions)
  What I will NOT do:            (take the decision back)

FAILURE
  What happens if it goes wrong — what I will do, in advance:

The last box matters more than the rest. If you have not decided in advance how you will behave when a delegated decision goes badly, you will behave the way you feel in the moment, which is to take it back — and the team will read the reversal, not the original delegation.

docs.title: 3. Delegating a decision, not just the work
docs.text:
The test of whether you delegated a decision is simple: could they make a choice you would not have made, and would it stand? If the answer is no, you delegated a recommendation.

Ana runs a 40-person operations function. She has told Priyanka to "own" the choice of a new shift-scheduling vendor. Two weeks later Priyanka arrives with a comparison and no decision.

Priyanka: Here are the three. Which do you want?

Ana: I said this was yours, and then I never said at what level, which is my mistake. Let me fix that now. This is level 5 — you decide, I'll give you my view if you want it, and I'll back whichever way you go, including if it's not the one I'd pick.

Priyanka: ...Okay. Do you want to give me the view?

Ana: Do you want it before or after you tell me yours?

Priyanka: After. Fine. I'd take Meridian. It's 15% more expensive and the interface is worse, but they'll do the data migration and the other two won't, and we don't have anyone to do a migration in Q3.

Ana: My instinct was the cheapest one, because I was looking at the annual cost and not at who does the migration. You've weighted a constraint I'd underweighted. Go with Meridian.

Priyanka: What if the migration slips and it looks bad?

Ana: Then it's a decision I backed. Here's what I'll actually do: if procurement or Finance push back, I'll tell them the choice was yours and that I support it — I won't distance myself. What I'd like in return is that you tell me early if it's going wrong, not late. Constraints I should have given you at the start: the ceiling is 90k a year, Legal has to see any contract over two years, and don't sign anything past March without me because of the budget cycle.

Priyanka: That's the first time I've had the actual number.

Note the two repairs. Ana names the level explicitly, and she states the constraints she had been holding in her head — the most common reason delegated decisions come back is that the person is guessing at boundaries nobody told them, and guessing conservatively means escalating.

docs.title: 4. Delegating upward conflict back down
docs.text:
The other capacity drain is being used as a channel between two people who could talk to each other. It feels like support and it is a habit you are training.

The rule: you carry the relationship, they carry the conversation. Absorb the conflict only when there is a genuine power asymmetry, when you have information they don't, or when it has already failed at their level twice.

Dan: Can you talk to Finance? They keep rejecting our purchase requests and Marta's impossible.

Ana: Tell me what's actually happening. What got rejected?

Dan: Three requests this month. The reason field just says "insufficient detail."

Ana: What did Marta say when you asked what detail she needs?

Dan: I haven't. She's rejected me three times, I'm not going to get a straight answer.

Ana: So the state of play is: three rejections, one hypothesis about her, and no conversation. If I go and ask her, what happens the fourth time it gets rejected?

Dan: ...I come back to you.

Ana: Right, and you've learned that the route to Finance is through me, which is worse for you than for me. Here's what I'll do and won't do. I won't have the conversation. I will tell you two things I know that you don't: Marta's team got audited in February and they're under instruction to document justification on everything, and she is not the one who wrote that rule. And I'll message her today saying you'll be in touch and that you have my backing on the spend. You ask her one question: "What would a request look like that you could approve first time?"

Dan: And if that goes nowhere?

Ana: Then come back and we look at it again — with what she said. If it's still stuck after you've tried properly, I'll go with you, not instead of you.

Ana gave Dan exactly what he lacked (context and air cover) and withheld exactly what he didn't (the conversation itself). She also set the condition for escalation in advance, so coming back isn't a defeat.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes
docs.text:
• Delegating the task, keeping the judgement. "Draft it and I'll review" every time is level 1 wearing a level 5 costume.
  • Taking it back on the first wobble. If you reverse a delegated decision, say why in terms of the contract — "this crossed a constraint I gave you" — not in terms of quality, or nobody will use their authority again.
  • Delegating without the information. People escalate because they are guessing at boundaries. Write the constraints down.
  • Dumping. Handing over work you find dull with no growth in it and calling it development is transparent, and it is noticed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
List every decision you personally made in the last two weeks. For each, write the level from section 1 that you actually operated at, and the level it could be at with the right constraints written down. Pick the one with the biggest gap and fill in the delegation contract in section 2 with that person this week — including the failure box.

Separately, count the times in the last month you were the messenger between two people who could have spoken directly. For the next one, use Ana's structure in section 4: give the context and the air cover, decline the conversation, and name in advance what would make escalation legitimate.

docs.title: 06 · Difficult Conversations
docs.text: The conversations you postpone are the ones that define you as a leader, because the whole team can see what you tolerate. The delay is never kindness — the person carries on doing the thing, the gap between their self-image and your view widens for months, and when it finally surfaces it arrives as a shock and often as an unfair one. "Why is this the first I'm hearing of it?" is a legitimate complaint about a real management failure. This module gives you a preparation worksheet, an opening script structure that avoids the two standard traps, and two worked conversations — one on behaviour, one on performance.

docs.title: 1. Why the opening sentence decides the outcome
docs.text:
Almost all difficult conversations fail in the first thirty seconds, in one of two directions.

Trap Sounds like What the other person hears The soft open "How's everything going? Great. Anyway, small thing…" Nothing is wrong. They leave unaware there was a message The verdict open "We need to talk about your attitude in meetings." I am on trial and the judgement is already made. Defence mode The sandwich Praise, criticism, praise The praise is a delivery mechanism, so future praise is now worthless

The alternative is what Stone, Patton and Heen call the third story: open with a description a neutral observer would recognise, which contains your concern but not your conclusion, and then invite their version before you give yours.

  • Verdict: "You've been dismissive of Rina in the last three meetings."
  • Third story: "I've noticed something in the last three planning meetings that I'd like to compare notes on — a few times Rina started a point and it didn't land, and I want to understand what's happening there from where you sit."

The second version says the same thing and leaves the conversation open. It is not softer; it is more precise.

docs.title: 2. The preparation worksheet
docs.text:
Do not improvise these. Twenty minutes of preparation is the difference between a conversation and an argument.

DIFFICULT CONVERSATION PREP

1. FACTS  (only what a camera would have recorded)
   Specific instances, with dates:
   What I actually observed vs. what I inferred:

2. IMPACT
   The concrete cost — to the work, to other people, to them:
   How do I know that impact is real and not my assumption?

3. THEIR STORY  (write it as if you were them, generously)
   What might make their behaviour completely reasonable?
   What pressure might they be under that I can't see?
   What might they say that would change my mind?

4. MY CONTRIBUTION  (there is nearly always one)
   What did I fail to say, and when should I have said it?
   What have I rewarded that I'm now criticising?

5. OUTCOME
   What must be different, specifically and observably:
   What is negotiable, and what genuinely is not:

6. OPENING SENTENCE  (write it out, word for word)
   ______________________________________________

7. LANDMINES
   What might they say that would knock me off course?
   My response if they cry / get angry / go silent:

Box 3 is the one people skip and the one that changes conversations. If you cannot construct a version of events in which the person is behaving reasonably, you have not prepared — you have rehearsed.

docs.title: 3. The conversation structure
docs.text:
Six moves, in order. The order is the method.

Move Purpose Wording 1. Signal Remove ambiguity about the register "I want to raise something that's been on my mind. It's not a crisis, and I'd rather say it than sit on it." 2. Third story Put the observable on the table "In the last three planning meetings, I noticed…" 3. Ask first Get their version before you conclude "What's your read on it?" — then actually listen (Level 1, Module 3) 4. State impact The cost, not the character "The effect is that we lose the objection early and pay for it late." 5. Own your part Restore symmetry "I should have said this after the first meeting, not the third." 6. Agree the change Specific, observable, dated "What would you do differently on Tuesday?"

The one non-negotiable: move 3 comes before move 4. If you deliver impact before hearing their version, everything after it is a defence of your judgement rather than a conversation about the work.

docs.title: 4. A worked conversation: behaviour
docs.text:
Rina is quiet in planning meetings. Tom, the most experienced person on the team, talks over her — Tom is well-regarded, works hard, and has no idea he is doing it. Their manager, Yusuf, has prepared the worksheet.

Yusuf: I want to raise something that's been on my mind for a couple of weeks. It's not a crisis, and I'd rather say it than sit on it. In the last three planning meetings I've watched Rina start a point and not finish it — twice you came in over the top of her, and once you summarised what she was saying before she got there. I want to compare notes, because I don't know what it looks like from where you're sitting.

Tom: Really? I— honestly, I thought I was helping. She takes a while to get to the point and we're always short on time.

Yusuf: Say more about the time pressure.

Tom: We've got 45 minutes and eleven items. I'm trying to keep it moving. And when Rina's uncertain about something she prefaces it a lot, so I jump in to speed it up.

Yusuf: That's useful — I'd assumed it was impatience with her and it sounds like it's impatience with the agenda. Here's the effect I'm seeing, though. In the last two meetings, Rina raised a concern about the regional rollout dates that got cut off. She was right. We found out three weeks later, from the region, and it cost us a fortnight. The thing she was slow to say was the thing we needed most.

Tom: ...I didn't know that's what she'd been saying.

Yusuf: And I should have raised this after the first meeting rather than the third. Some of this is my agenda — eleven items in 45 minutes is my design, and it's creating the pressure you're responding to. I'll cut that to six.

Tom: That would genuinely help.

Yusuf: What would you do differently on Tuesday?

Tom: Not interrupt, obviously. But if I just sit on it I'll be counting the seconds. Could I ask her directly at the point where she matters — "Rina, what's the regional view?" — rather than waiting and then jumping in?

Yusuf: That's better than what I was going to suggest. Do that. I'll watch on Tuesday and tell you afterwards what I saw, either way.

Yusuf changed his own meeting design in move 5, which is why Tom could accept move 4 without defending himself. He also got a better solution than the one he'd prepared, because he ran move 3 properly.

docs.title: 5. A worked conversation: performance
docs.text:
Different case — repeated missed commitments, third occurrence, and the message must be unmistakable. Here the third story does not mean softening the standard.

Yusuf: This is a serious conversation and I want you to hear it clearly. The monthly regional pack has been late three months running — the 9th, the 11th and the 12th, against a due date of the 5th. Each time I heard about it after the deadline, from someone else. What's going on?

Marc: The inputs from the two new regions come in late. I've been chasing them.

Yusuf: How long has that been true?

Marc: Since they onboarded. About four months.

Yusuf: Then I want to separate two things, because they need different fixes. The input delay is a real problem and I'll help with it — I can go to the regional leads this week. The part that's yours is that for four months you knew there was a structural problem, and you didn't tell me. Three times I found out after the fact. That's the thing that has to change, and it isn't negotiable.

Marc: I thought I could fix it before it became a thing.

Yusuf: I understand the instinct, and I'd rather have the flag. So, specifically: the pack is due on the 5th. If it's at risk, I hear about it on the 1st, from you, with what you need. If the inputs are still the blocker after I've talked to the regional leads, we change the due date rather than miss it. If the next two months are late and unflagged, we're in a different conversation about the role, and I want to be straight with you that that's where this goes.

Marc: Understood. The 1st.

Yusuf: I'll put those dates in writing today so neither of us is working from memory. And I'll come back to you on Friday about the regional leads — that's my commitment in this.

Two things to copy. Yusuf separated the systemic cause from the behavioural one, so Marc could not use the real input problem to absorb the whole conversation. And he named the consequence explicitly — a difficult conversation in which the person leaves unaware that their job is at stake has not been had.

docs.title: 6. Landmines
docs.text:
• Tears or anger. Pause, don't retract. "Take a minute. I'm not going anywhere, and I'm not withdrawing what I said."
  • "Who told you this?" Speak only to what you observed yourself, and if you can't, don't raise it until you can.
  • Counter-attack. Note it, park it, finish yours. "That's a fair thing to raise and I want to hear it properly — let's finish this first, then I'll take it seriously."
  • Total agreement. Suspiciously fast agreement usually means escape. Ask "what will you actually do differently?" and listen for specifics.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Name the conversation you have been avoiding — the one that surfaced in your mind while reading this. Complete the worksheet in section 2 for it, in full, including box 3 and box 4. Write your opening sentence word for word and read it aloud; if it contains a verdict or a diagnosis of character, rewrite it as an observation until it doesn't.

Then schedule it, inside seven days. Afterwards, write down two things: what you learned in move 3 that you did not know, and whether you got to move 6 with a specific dated commitment or settled for general agreement.

docs.title: 07 · Leading Through Change
docs.text: Reorganisations, new systems, budget cuts, a merged team, a strategy pivot — the announcement takes ten minutes and the disruption takes six months. Most managers treat the gap between those two numbers as an inconvenience to be minimised with enthusiasm. It isn't: it is the actual work. Your team is not resisting the org chart, they are processing the loss of a way of working that they were good at, and enthusiasm aimed at people who are grieving competence reads as contempt. This module gives you the transition model that explains the gap, a communication plan template, a script for the announcement, and a worked example of the conversation that follows it.

docs.title: 1. Change is external; transition is internal
docs.text:
William Bridges' distinction is the most practically useful idea in this whole area. Change is the event: the new structure exists from the 1st. Transition is the psychological process people go through to let go of the old and commit to the new, and it starts later than the change and finishes much later.

Phase What people feel What they do What they need from you Ending Loss, anger, denial; grief for competence and status Relitigate the decision; talk about how it used to work Acknowledge the loss by name. Say what is actually ending, and what isn't Neutral zone Confusion, low productivity, anxiety, some creativity Ask the same questions repeatedly; over-interpret small signals Short-term goals, high-frequency communication, tolerance for the dip New beginning Cautious energy; identification with the new way Take initiative; stop referencing the old structure Quick wins made visible, and the new purpose stated in their terms

Three consequences that follow directly:

  • The dip is real and is not a morale problem. Expect reduced output in the neutral zone and plan for it rather than pushing harder into it.
  • You are ahead of them, always. You have known about this for six weeks. Day one for them is week six for you, and the most common leadership failure in change is impatience born of forgetting that.
  • You cannot skip the ending. A leader who opens with "this is a huge opportunity" before naming what's being lost is asking people to begin before they have finished, and they will simply not follow.

docs.title: 2. The four questions everyone is actually asking
docs.text:
Whatever the strategic rationale, every individual is running four questions, in this order, and will not hear anything else until they are answered.

  1. What happens to me? Role, manager, team, location, pay.
  2. Why is this happening? In plain terms, not strategy-deck terms.
  3. When will I know? A date, even if the date is "I'll know by the 14th and will tell you the same day."
  4. What is staying the same? Continuity is what makes change survivable, and nobody ever mentions it.

Question 4 is the one leaders omit entirely. "Your team, your clients and your manager are unchanged; what changes is who approves spend" cuts the perceived size of a change in half, truthfully.

docs.title: 3. Change communication plan
docs.text:
CHANGE COMMUNICATION PLAN
Change: ______________________  Announced: ______  Effective: ______

WHAT IS ENDING
  Ways of working that stop:
  What people will lose (status, expertise, relationships, autonomy):
  Who loses the most, by name:
  What I will say explicitly about that loss:

WHAT IS NOT CHANGING
  (list at least three concrete things)

THE FOUR QUESTIONS — my answer to each, in one sentence
  What happens to me:
  Why:
  When will I know:
  What stays the same:

WHAT I DON'T KNOW YET
  Open questions:
  The date by which I'll have each answer:
  (Never fill this section with "nothing" — nobody believes it)

SEQUENCE
  Told individually first (most affected):
  Told in team meeting:
  Told by someone else / broadcast:
  Order and timing:  (nobody hears it first from a group email)

CADENCE THROUGH THE NEUTRAL ZONE
  Update rhythm:                 (weekly minimum, even with no news)
  Standing "no news this week" message: yes / no
  Short-term goal for the next 4 weeks:
  What quick win will I make visible, and when:

The "what I don't know yet" box is what buys you credibility. A manager who admits three open questions and then answers them on the promised date is trusted; a manager who projects total certainty is discounted the first time reality diverges.

docs.title: 4. The announcement
docs.text:
Marisa leads a nine-person market research team. Following a merger, the team is being split: four people move into a central insights function under a different director, five stay with her doing a narrower brief. She has known for five weeks. She has already spoken to the four movers individually, the day before. This is the team meeting.

Marisa: I'm going to tell you the decision, then what I know, then what I don't, and then we'll have as long as you want for questions.

Marisa: From the 1st of next month, market research splits. Nikhil, Aisha, Tom and Ben move into the central insights function reporting to Deepa. Sara, Ravi, Lena, Marco and I stay in the commercial team and our brief narrows to pricing and product research. I spoke to everyone moving yesterday, so nobody in this room is hearing their own situation for the first time right now.

Marisa: Before the rationale, let me say what's ending, because I think it's the bigger thing. This team has worked together for three years and we are unusually good at handing work between us — that specific thing, the way we cover each other, does not survive this. I don't want to pretend otherwise or call it an opportunity. It's a real loss and I'm sorry about it.

Marisa: The why: the merged organisation has three research teams asking the same panels the same questions, and the duplication is genuinely costing money. I argued for keeping the team whole and I lost that argument. I still think the central function is the right call overall, and I want to be honest that both of those are true.

Marisa: What isn't changing: no roles are at risk and no pay is changing in this reorg. Everyone keeps their current projects to completion. Our Tuesday session stays, for everyone, for at least six months, and I'll keep running it.

Marisa: What I don't know: where the four of you will sit physically, whether the panel budget follows you, and what happens to the retail tracker after Q3. I'll have the first two by the 14th and I'll tell you the day I know, including if the answer is still no answer. The tracker I genuinely don't know and won't pretend to.

Aisha: Is this the first stage of something bigger?

Marisa: I don't know, and I won't tell you it isn't. What I can tell you is what I've been told, which is that there is no second phase planned this year, and that I'll say so plainly if that changes.

Ravi: Do we get a say in who goes where?

Marisa: No — that's decided. I'd rather tell you that than run a consultation that isn't one.

docs.title: 5. The neutral zone conversation
docs.text:
Three weeks later. Tom, one of the movers, is visibly disengaged.

Marisa: How are you finding it?

Tom: Fine. It's fine.

Marisa: I'll go first, then. Three weeks in, I'm finding it worse than I expected. I keep starting to ask you something and remembering it's not mine to ask.

Tom: ...Honestly, I don't know what I'm for at the moment. I was the person who knew the retail panel end to end. In the central team there are two other people who know it, and one of them knows it better. So what am I bringing?

Marisa: That's the actual thing, isn't it. Not the reporting line — the expertise not being scarce any more.

Tom: Yeah. I sound pathetic.

Marisa: You sound like someone who lost the thing that made him valuable, three weeks ago. That's the normal middle of this and it doesn't mean it stays this way. Can I ask a different question — what do you know that those two people don't?

Tom: Commercial context. They've never sat with a pricing team. They can run the panel; they can't tell you which question the business will act on.

Marisa: That's a real and rare thing, and it's the bridge between the two teams. What would it take for Deepa to know you have it?

Tom: She doesn't. I've been quiet in her meetings.

Marisa: What's one thing in the next two weeks?

Tom: There's a brief going out on the loyalty study. I could rewrite the question set from a commercial angle and send it to her with the reasoning.

Marisa: Do that, and copy me — not to approve it, just so I can tell Deepa what you're bringing. I'll do that this week either way.

Marisa did not reassure, minimise, or sell the change. She named the loss precisely (scarcity of expertise, not the reporting line), gave a short-term goal, and used her position to make him visible. That is the whole job in the neutral zone.

docs.title: 6. Failure modes
docs.text:
• Announcing to a group before telling the most affected. Nobody should hear their own fate in a room of nine people.
  • Relentless positivity. Enthusiasm without acknowledged loss reads as either dishonest or oblivious, and costs you the trust you need later.
  • Going quiet when there's no news. Silence gets filled with the worst available theory. A weekly "nothing new, next update Friday" is a real communication.
  • Pretending you agreed. If you argued and lost, you may say so without dissent — "I argued for X, I lost, and I'm implementing this properly" is honest and loyal at the same time. What you may not do is privately disown it while publicly delivering it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Take a change your team is living through now, or one you know is coming, and fill in the plan in section 3 — especially "what is ending" and "who loses the most, by name." For each named person, write the specific thing they are losing: expertise that stops being scarce, a relationship, autonomy, an identity as the person who knows X.

Then have one conversation this week with the person who loses the most, using Marisa's structure in section 5: go first with something honest, name the loss precisely rather than generally, agree one short-term concrete goal for the next fortnight, and commit to one thing you will do with your own visibility to help them.

docs.title: 08 · Recognizing & Developing Talent
docs.text: Most managers identify talent by noticing who reminds them of themselves, and then develop it by sending that person on a course. Both halves are wrong. The first produces a team that is demographically and cognitively narrow and quietly demoralised; the second produces a certificate and no change in behaviour. Recognising talent is a discipline of looking for specific observable signals — several of which look like inconvenience — and developing it is mostly about the work you assign, not the training you buy. This module gives you a performance and potential grid, a signal checklist, a development plan template built on the 70/20/10 split, and a worked development conversation.

docs.title: 1. Performance is not potential
docs.text:
The most expensive confusion in talent management. Performance is delivery in the current role; potential is capacity to succeed in a materially different one. They correlate weakly, and treating them as the same thing is how organisations promote their best individual contributor into a mediocre manager and lose both.

Low potential signal High potential signal High performance Core strength. Excellent where they are. Deepen, reward, do not push upward against their wishes Grow. Stretch now, or they leave within a year Low performance Address. Module 6 conversation — role fit or performance Investigate. Almost always a fixable cause: wrong role, bad fit with you, unclear expectations, life circumstances

Two notes on using this honestly. The "core strength" box is not a consolation prize — a team of people brilliant and content in their current roles is a functional team, and pressuring them into management because it is the only visible progression is a failure of your career ladder, not of them. And the "investigate" box is where most overlooked talent sits; low performance is a symptom with many causes, and only one of them is capability.

docs.title: 2. Signals of potential you can actually observe
docs.text:
Not "shows leadership." These are behaviours you can point to with a date attached.

Signal What it looks like concretely Why it predicts Learning agility Changes their approach after feedback within weeks, not months The single strongest predictor of success in an unfamiliar role Asks about the why Wants the business reason behind a task, not just the task Will make good decisions when you're not there Seeks disconfirmation Goes and finds out where they're wrong; changes their mind out loud Won't defend a failing plan to protect their ego Scope creep, the good kind Notices adjacent problems and fixes them unasked Already operating a level up Teaches Others go to them, informally, and leave abler Multiplier, not just a producer Handles ambiguity Makes progress with incomplete information rather than waiting Senior roles are mostly incomplete information Takes the unglamorous job Volunteers for the necessary, unrewarded thing Ownership rather than positioning

And the signals that mislead, which is the harder half of this list:

  • Confidence. Reads as potential and predicts almost nothing.
  • Visibility. Being in the room with you is a function of geography and personality. Some of your strongest people are on a different site, in a different timezone, or simply quiet.
  • Similarity to you. The most reliably distorting bias in this whole area. If your list of high-potentials all share your background, communication style or working pattern, the list is wrong.
  • Long hours. Measures availability, not capability, and frequently measures poor delegation.

A cheap corrective: for each direct report, write down one instance of a potential signal from the table above with a date. Whoever you cannot fill in is not necessarily low-potential — they may just be someone you have not been watching.

docs.title: 3. The development plan
docs.text:
Development is 70% challenging work, 20% people, 10% formal learning. Most plans invert this, because the 10% is the only part with a budget code. Build the plan from the assignment backwards.

DEVELOPMENT PLAN
Person: ______________  Period: __________  Reviewed: __________

WHERE THEY WANT TO GO
  In their words (not my paraphrase):
  What they want that I know the organisation can't give:

STRENGTH TO DEEPEN
  The thing they are unusually good at:
  How the next 6 months makes them more so:

THE ONE GAP THAT MATTERS
  (Only one. A plan with four gaps develops nothing)
  The gap, stated behaviourally:
  What "closed" would look like, observably:

70 · THE WORK
  Stretch assignment that requires the gap to close:
  What could genuinely go wrong, and what I'll do about it:
  Decision rights (see Module 5 level 1-7):  ____

20 · THE PEOPLE
  Who they should be exposed to, and how I'll arrange it:
  Who mentors, and on what specifically:
  What I will do to make their work visible upward:

10 · FORMAL
  Course/reading/certification, if any — and what it's FOR:

CHECKPOINTS
  Dates:                Format:
  How we'll know it worked (observable, not "feels better"):

The "what could go wrong" box is the difference between a stretch assignment and a trap. A stretch that fails publicly with no cover from you is not development; it is an expensive lesson in not volunteering.

docs.title: 4. A worked development conversation
docs.text:
Hana manages a customer support function. Joel is her steadiest agent — high performance, three years in role, never puts himself forward, regularly ignored in talent reviews because he is quiet and works from a regional office. Hana has noticed three signals: new joiners informally go to him, he rewrote the refund guidance nobody asked him to touch, and he changed his approach to escalations within two weeks of one piece of feedback.

Hana: I want to talk about the next couple of years rather than this month's numbers. Where do you actually want to go? Not the version you think I want to hear.

Joel: Honestly, I don't know. I've been asked if I want to manage and I don't think I do. Which I assume means I'm stuck.

Hana: It doesn't, and I want to separate two things. Do you not want to manage, or do you not want to stop doing the work?

Joel: The second one. The managers here spend all day in meetings about the work and never touch it. That looks miserable to me.

Hana: That's useful, because there's a direction that isn't management. Can I tell you what I've actually observed? Three things. Every new starter in the last year has ended up asking you things rather than their buddy. You rewrote the refund guidance in March without being asked, and it's the version everyone uses now. And after we talked about escalation tone in February, your escalations changed inside two weeks — that one is rarer than you'd think.

Joel: I didn't think anyone noticed the refund thing.

Hana: It's the reason we're having this conversation. So the strength is that you make other people better at the work, and you improve the work itself. The gap — and there's only one I care about — is that all of that happens in a five-metre radius around your desk. You've never presented anything, never sat in a cross-functional forum, and nobody outside this office knows your name. That's what stops you being a principal-level specialist rather than a senior agent.

Joel: That's fair. The presenting part is genuinely unappealing.

Hana: Then let's make it as small as possible and real rather than practising. Here's what I'd propose for the next six months. The work: you own the redesign of the whole escalation playbook — that's your call at level 5, meaning you decide and I back it, and it needs sign off from Ops and Legal, which means you'll have to explain it to people who don't work here. The people: I'll introduce you to Sanjay in Ops, and I'd like Priya to mentor you on one specific thing, which is how she runs a room she doesn't chair. And I'll do this — every time the playbook comes up in my director's meeting, I'll say it's yours and I'll have you present it once, in the last month, not the first.

Joel: What happens if Legal blocks the whole thing?

Hana: Then we do it together and I say publicly it was my scoping that missed the constraint, because that will be true. What I won't do is take it back off you halfway.

Joel: What's the formal bit? There's usually a course.

Hana: Only if you want one, and only for something specific. There's a half-day on facilitating workshops that would actually be used in month four. That's it — I'm not sending you on anything to tick a box.

Note what makes this a plan rather than a chat: one gap, an assignment that cannot be completed without closing it, a named delegation level, a named mentor with a specific subject, an explicit commitment about visibility, and a stated failure position.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes
docs.text:
• The nine-box as a verdict. Grids are for prompting a conversation about a person, not for stamping them. Position changes with role, manager and life stage; re-examine at least annually.
  • Development plans nobody re-reads. A plan with no checkpoint date is a document, not a plan. Put the review in both calendars now.
  • Developing only the visible. Set yourself the test in section 2 — one dated signal per person. The blanks are your blind spots.
  • Promising what you can't deliver. Never imply a promotion you do not control. Say what you will do — advocate, assign, make visible — and be explicit about what is not yours to give.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Place every direct report on the grid in section 1, then justify each placement with one dated observation from the table in section 2. Any placement you cannot evidence is an impression, not an assessment — mark those, because they are where your biases live.

Then pick one person, ideally from the "investigate" box or someone you rarely see, and build the plan in section 3 with them — in a conversation, not beforehand. Hold yourself to two constraints: exactly one gap, and the 70% assignment must be work that already needs doing, not an exercise invented for their benefit. Book the first checkpoint before you leave the room.

docs.title: 09 · Servant Leadership in Meetings
docs.text: Meetings are where your leadership is most visible and least examined. Everything from Levels 1 and 2 — listening, safety, conflict, coaching — either shows up in the room or is theoretical. The default pattern is well known: the most senior person states a view first, the same two people speak, everyone else calibrates to what has already been said, and the meeting produces agreement that dissolves the moment people leave. Serving the group's thinking means designing the meeting so the information in the quietest heads reaches the decision. This module gives you a meeting design canvas, a facilitation move set, and a worked before-and-after of the same meeting run two ways.

docs.title: 1. One meeting, one job
docs.text:
Most bad meetings are two or three meetings wearing a trenchcoat. Name the type before you write the agenda, and never run two types in one block without a hard break between them.

Type Output Right format Fatal mistake Inform Shared understanding Written first, meeting only for questions Reading slides aloud to people who can read Generate A wide set of options Silent generation, then build Starting with open discussion — first idea anchors everything Decide A named decision with an owner and date Options pre-circulated, decision rights stated up front Discovering mid-meeting that nobody knows who decides Build Alignment and commitment Small group, real work done in the room Inviting an audience Connect Relationship and trust Unstructured, protected time Adding an agenda and killing the point

The single highest-value question to ask before any meeting you call: what will be true at the end that isn't true now? If you can't answer it in one sentence, cancel and send a note.

docs.title: 2. The meeting design canvas
docs.text:
MEETING DESIGN CANVAS

Type (one only):  inform / generate / decide / build / connect
What is true at the end that isn't true now:
  ____________________________________________

DECISION RIGHTS  (state these out loud at the start)
  Who decides:
  Who must be consulted (their input changes the outcome):
  Who is informed (present for context, not for a vote):
  Is this actually already decided?  yes / no
    If yes, this is an INFORM meeting. Say so and don't fake a debate.

ATTENDEES
  Name — why they are here — what happens if they aren't:
  (No answer to column three = remove them and send the notes)

PRE-WORK
  What is circulated, and when (24h minimum):
  What people should arrive having done:

DESIGN
  First 5 minutes:            (silent read / silent write / round)
  How the quiet people get airtime:
  When I speak:               (target: last, on any question I own)
  How dissent is invited:     (specific mechanism, not "any concerns?")

CLOSE
  Decision, owner, date — read aloud before anyone leaves:
  What I will send in writing, and by when:
  Who was not in the room and needs to hear it from me directly:

docs.title: 3. Facilitation moves
docs.text:
Techniques with mechanisms, not exhortations.

Move How What it fixes Speak last Withhold your view until everyone with a view has given theirs Anchoring on the senior voice — the biggest single distortion in the room Silent start Five minutes reading the doc or writing options, in the room, no talking Meetings where only the fast talkers and the pre-prepared contribute Brainwriting Everyone writes three options privately before any discussion First-idea anchoring in generate meetings Round Go round the table by name, everyone says one thing, no cross-talk The same two people occupying 80% of airtime Named dissent "I want the strongest argument against this — Ravi, you go first" Groupthink; makes objecting the assigned task rather than a risky act Airtime count Tally who spoke, privately, for one meeting Your own inaccurate sense of how balanced the discussion was Process, not content "We've been on this ten minutes with no new information — decide or park?" Meetings that drift and end at the time limit rather than at an answer Read-back close State decision, owner and date aloud before anyone leaves Meetings that "agreed" and produce nothing

Speak last is the whole module in one habit. If you state your view first, the rest of the meeting is a referendum on you, and you will mistake compliance for consensus.

docs.title: 4. Same meeting, two ways
docs.text:
A decision meeting: whether to move customer onboarding from the sales team to the support team. Convener is Dara, the director. Present: Ines (sales lead), Kwame (support lead), Bea (ops analyst), Tunde (new regional manager, four weeks in).

Version one, the default

Dara: Thanks all. So — I've looked at this and I think onboarding clearly belongs in support. Sales shouldn't be doing implementation. Thoughts?

Kwame: Agreed, makes sense.

Ines: I mean — if that's the direction, we'd need headcount to move with it, but yes, I can see it.

Dara: Bea?

Bea: No objections from me.

Dara: Tunde?

Tunde: Happy to go with the room.

Dara: Great, that was easy. Let's do it.

Eight minutes, unanimous, and worthless. Dara anchored in sentence one, so nobody after her was giving a view — they were responding to hers. Bea has churn data showing onboarding quality drives first-year renewal. Tunde has watched this exact move fail at his previous employer. Neither piece of information reached the decision.

Version two, designed

Dara: Decision today: where onboarding sits from Q3. To be clear up front about rights — I decide, but Ines and Kwame's input changes the outcome because it's their headcount, and Bea and Tunde are here because they know things I don't. This is not pre-decided; if it were I'd tell you.

Dara: Five minutes, silently, on the doc I sent. Write down the single strongest argument for each option, including the one you don't favour. Then we'll go round.

(Five minutes.)

Dara: Round. Tunde first — you're newest, so you're least contaminated by how we've always done it.

Tunde: At my last company we made this exact move. It failed, and the reason was specific: support was measured on ticket closure time, and onboarding is slow work. Within two quarters they'd deprioritised it into nothing. The structure wasn't the problem, the metric was.

Bea: Mine's the other direction. Accounts with an onboarding quality score above 7 renew at 91%; below 4, it's 62%. That's the largest single lever in the renewal number, and right now nobody owns that score.

Kwame: My argument for taking it: my team already picks up the failures at month three, blind, with no context. My argument against: Tunde is right about the metric, and I'd be signing up for work my current targets punish me for doing.

Ines: My argument for keeping it: relationship continuity through the first 90 days. My argument against — and this is uncomfortable — my reps are compensated on new bookings, so onboarding is the thing they do last. I'd be defending a structure my own comp plan undermines.

Dara: Now mine, and you'll notice it's changed. I came in convinced this was a structural question. Three of you have told me it's a measurement question — both teams are incentivised against doing it well, so moving it just relocates the problem.

Dara: Strongest argument against moving it, then. Kwame, you go — you're the one who'd gain the team.

Kwame: That we spend two quarters on a reorg and land exactly where we are, with a worse handover.

Dara: That's persuasive. Here's the decision: onboarding moves to support from Q3, and it moves with a dedicated onboarding quality metric that is not ticket closure time — Bea's score, owned by Kwame, reported alongside renewal. Ines, two of your onboarding specialists move with it; I'll fund the third from my budget rather than take it from your quota headcount. Owner of the transition plan: Kwame, with Bea. First draft by the 20th.

Dara: Read-back so nobody leaves with a different version. Move to support, Q3, new metric replaces closure time for that work, two heads move plus one funded by me, Kwame owns the plan, draft on the 20th. Anything I've got wrong? ... I'll send that in writing today, and I'll talk to the two specialists myself before it's announced.

Twenty-five minutes instead of eight, a materially better decision, and the person four weeks into the company supplied the insight that changed it — because he was asked first, before anyone senior had spoken.

docs.title: 5. Meetings you attend but don't run
docs.text:
Servant leadership in someone else's meeting is mostly restraint plus one or two well-placed moves.

  • Give your view late even when you're not chairing. Your seniority anchors regardless of who called the meeting.
  • Redirect credit and questions. "That analysis is Bea's, and she's in the room" costs you nothing and changes what happens next.
  • Name the process, not the content. "Can I check who's deciding this?" is the single most useful sentence available to a participant.
  • Amplify a cut-off point. "I want to come back to what Rina started to say" — a five-word intervention that changes who gets heard.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Take the next meeting you own and fill in the canvas in section 2 before you send the invite. Force yourself through two boxes honestly: for each attendee, what happens if they aren't there; and whether the thing is already decided. If it is, convert the meeting to an inform and say so out loud — faking a consultation is one of the fastest ways to lose the trust you built in Level 1.

In the meeting itself, use exactly two moves from section 3: speak last on any question you own, and one of silent start, round, or named dissent. Keep a private airtime tally as you go. Afterwards, write down who spoke least, what they said when they finally did, and whether the outcome differed from what you would have decided in the first two minutes. If it never differs, you are chairing a ratification process rather than a decision.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Coaching Plan for a Direct Report
docs.text: Everything in this level converges here. A coaching plan is not a development form filed with HR; it is a working document you build with one real person, that commits both of you to specific things, and that you are still using in three months. The test of whether you have completed this level is not whether you can describe GROW — it is whether one person on your team can now do something in October that they could not do in July, and whether they would describe the plan as theirs. This module gives you the deliverable spec, a fully worked example, the first coaching session that produced it, and a rubric to mark your own against.

docs.title: 1. The brief
docs.text:
Choose one direct report — not your strongest, not your weakest. The right subject is someone in the middle whose growth would materially change what your team can do, and who you have quietly been under- investing in.

Produce a written plan containing all eight sections in the template below, built across two conversations rather than in one sitting. Section by section, this level supplies the method:

Plan section Module Goal, in their words 01 · GROW, Goal stage Current reality, evidenced 01 · GROW, Reality stage + 08 · signals The one gap 08 · Recognizing & Developing Talent The stretch assignment 05 · Delegation, levels 1-7 The conversation they're avoiding 06 · Difficult Conversations Support and exposure 08 · the 20% What I will change about me 03 · Psychological safety + 09 · Meetings Checkpoints 01 · Way Forward

Two hard rules. One gap only — a plan naming four development areas develops none of them. And the person must be able to state the goal in their own words, without you prompting, at the second checkpoint; if they can't, it was your plan.

docs.title: 2. The plan template
docs.text:
COACHING PLAN
Person: ______________  Role: ______________
Period: ______ to ______   Written with them on: ______

1. GOAL  (their words, quoted, not paraphrased)
   "..."
   What good looks like in 6 months, observably:
   Whose goal this is — evidence it's theirs:

2. REALITY  (facts with dates; strengths and gaps both)
   What they do unusually well:
   What is demonstrably not working, with instances:
   What they've already tried:
   What I got wrong that contributed:

3. THE ONE GAP
   Stated as a behaviour, not a trait:
   What "closed" looks like, observably:
   Why this gap and not the others:

4. THE STRETCH ASSIGNMENT  (70%)
   Real work, already needed by the business:
   Why it cannot be completed without closing the gap:
   Delegation level (1-7):  ____
   Constraints, exhaustively:
   What could go wrong and what I will do — decided in advance:

5. THE CONVERSATION THEY'RE AVOIDING
   Who, about what:
   Their prepared opening sentence:
   My role: rehearse / observe / stay out — and which, explicitly:

6. SUPPORT AND EXPOSURE  (20% / 10%)
   Who mentors, on what specific thing:
   Rooms I will get them into:
   What I will say about them, to whom, and when:
   Formal learning, only if it serves the assignment:

7. WHAT I WILL CHANGE ABOUT MY OWN BEHAVIOUR
   Specific, observable, and they may hold me to it:

8. CHECKPOINTS
   Dates in both calendars:
   What we review:
   Signal that the plan is wrong and needs rewriting:

docs.title: 3. Worked example
docs.text:
Subject. Daniel Okoro, Senior Coordinator, promoted four months ago to lead a five-person facilities and workplace services team, from within the team. Delivery is fine. Two things are not: he is doing large amounts of the team's operational work himself at night, and one of his reports, Cal, has missed the weekly building compliance walkthrough three times without consequence. Daniel used to be Cal's peer and they are friends. His manager is Priya, head of workplace operations.

COACHING PLAN
Person: Daniel Okoro   Role: Senior Coordinator (team lead, 5 reports)
Period: 1 August to 31 January   Written with them on: 4 August

1. GOAL  (his words)
   "I want to stop being the person who catches everything, and be
    the person the team doesn't need to be caught by."
   6 months, observably: Daniel takes two consecutive weeks of leave
     with no work contact; the compliance walkthrough happens weekly
     without him doing it or chasing it.
   Whose goal: his. He raised the leave point unprompted — he
     cancelled leave twice this year and named it himself.

2. REALITY
   Does unusually well: relationships across the building; every
     contractor and every floor lead trusts him. Compliance record
     was the best in the region for two years running.
   Not working, with instances:
     - 12 Jun, 3 Jul, 24 Jul: he completed the walkthrough himself
       after Cal missed it, out of hours, and logged it under Cal's
       name. He has never told Cal he did this.
     - Team meeting 17 Jul: he answered all seven questions himself,
       including three that were directed at other people.
     - Timesheet system shows a mean of 51h/week since promotion.
   Already tried: a written rota (still bypasses it himself); asking
     Cal "is everything alright?" twice, receiving "yeah, fine."
   What I got wrong: I promoted him and gave him no delegation
     conversation at all. I have also praised him three times for
     "picking things up," which rewarded the exact behaviour I now
     want him to stop. That is my contribution and I said so to him.

3. THE ONE GAP
   Behaviour: when work is at risk, Daniel absorbs it himself rather
     than making the risk visible to the person who owns it.
   Closed looks like: a missed commitment by a team member results
     in a conversation with that person within 48 hours, and does
     not result in Daniel doing the task.
   Why this gap: every other issue — the hours, the meeting
     dominance, Cal's performance, his own leave — is downstream of
     this single behaviour. Fixing it fixes four things.

4. STRETCH ASSIGNMENT  (70%)
   Real work: own the Q4 relocation of the third floor, end to end —
     budget 140k, six weeks, four contractors, 90 staff moving.
     This is work the business needs and I would otherwise do.
   Why it forces the gap: it is physically impossible to absorb.
     He cannot personally do a floor move at night. He must
     distribute it and hold people to dates, including Cal.
   Delegation level: 5 (he decides; my view available on request;
     I back his call publicly, including to the directors).
   Constraints: 140k ceiling; Legal reviews any contract over 12
     months; the move weekend cannot be the 14th (audit); anything
     affecting building access comes to me before it's committed.
   What could go wrong: a contractor slips and the move overruns.
     Decided in advance — I do not take the project back. I take
     the escalation to the directors *with* him, and I say publicly
     that the scope was mine. I will not reverse his decisions;
     if one crosses a constraint above, I say that specifically
     rather than criticising the judgement.

5. THE CONVERSATION HE'S AVOIDING
   Who/what: Cal, three missed compliance walkthroughs, plus the
     fact that Daniel covered them silently and logged them under
     Cal's name — which Cal does not know.
   His opening sentence (his draft, third attempt):
     "I need to tell you something I should have said in June. The
      last three Thursday walkthroughs — I did them, after hours,
      and logged them as yours. That was wrong of me and it's why
      you've had no idea this was a problem. I want to fix both
      halves of that."
   My role: rehearse only. I ran the Module 6 worksheet with him,
     including box 3 — what might make Cal's behaviour reasonable.
     He discovered he had never asked. I am not in the room and I
     will not follow up with Cal myself.

6. SUPPORT AND EXPOSURE
   Mentor: Ines (regional facilities lead) on one specific thing —
     how she runs contractor negotiations she doesn't have authority
     over. Two sessions, booked, not open-ended.
   Rooms: he presents the relocation plan at the November directors'
     meeting. Not the first month — the last.
   What I will say, to whom, when: at the September ops leads
     meeting I will state that the relocation is Daniel's decision
     and that I am not the approver. Directors, same message,
     October.
   Formal: half-day on scheduling/critical path, in September only
     because the relocation needs it. Nothing else.

7. WHAT I WILL CHANGE
   - I stop praising out-of-hours rescue work. If I hear about it,
     I ask what it prevented someone else from learning.
   - In our 1:1s I will not answer any operational question for the
     first twenty minutes. I will ask what he's tried.
   - I will not accept a piece of work back from him during the
     relocation, even if he offers it and even if it's faster.
   He has permission to name it out loud when I break these.

8. CHECKPOINTS
   Dates: 1 Sep, 1 Oct, 5 Nov (post-relocation), 15 Jan. In both
     calendars now.
   Review: the two observable measures in section 1, plus one
     instance since last time where he made a risk visible instead
     of absorbing it.
   Plan is wrong if: by 1 Oct the relocation has become another
     thing he is doing alone at night. That means the assignment
     was too absorbable and we change it, not him.

docs.title: 4. The session that produced it
docs.text:
An excerpt from the first conversation, run on the GROW worksheet from Module 1. Priya's goal is that the plan is Daniel's, not hers.

Priya (Goal): Forget the team for a second. What do you want to be different by January?

Daniel: Fewer late nights, I suppose.

Priya: Is that the goal, or a symptom of it?

Daniel: ...Symptom. I want to stop being the person who catches everything. Be the person the team doesn't need to be caught by.

Priya (Reality): Give me the last time you caught something.

Daniel: Thursday. Cal missed the compliance walkthrough, so I did it at half seven.

Priya: And logged it how?

Daniel: ...Under his name.

Priya: How many times?

Daniel: Three.

Priya: What does Cal know about any of this?

Daniel: Nothing. That's the bit I've been trying not to look at.

Priya: What have you tried?

Daniel: A rota, which I then went round myself. And asking him twice if he was okay, and getting "fine" both times.

Priya: What do you think is going on with him? Give me the version where Cal is being completely reasonable.

Daniel: ...I don't have one. I've never actually asked him what's happening on Thursdays. His shift changed in May, now I say it out loud.

Priya (Options): So what could you do?

Daniel: Tell him.

Priya: What else?

Daniel: Move the walkthrough to a day that works, if the shift is the issue. Give it to someone else entirely.

Priya: What else? Even a bad one.

Daniel: Keep covering it and say nothing, which is what I've been doing. Or escalate it to you and let you deal with it.

Priya: Which of those actually gets you to January?

Daniel: Telling him. Including the part where I logged it under his name, which is going to be horrible.

Priya (Way forward): By when?

Daniel: This week. Thursday, before the next one.

Priya: Scale of one to ten, how likely is Thursday?

Daniel: Five. He's a friend and I've let this run for two months.

Priya: What would make it a nine?

Daniel: Writing the first sentence down and not improvising it. And booking it in the calendar now so I can't drift.

Priya: Do both. What do you want from me?

Daniel: Don't talk to Cal. If you fix it, I'm back where I started.

Priya: Agreed, and I'll say the same if he comes to me.

Priya contributed no content: not the shift change, not the rota, not the opening sentence. She contributed the sequence, one question about Cal's reasonableness, and the 1-10 check that converted a vague intention into a dated one.

docs.title: 5. Rubric — mark your own plan
docs.text:
Criterion Weak Strong Goal ownership You wrote it; they'd paraphrase it differently Quoted in their words; they raised it first Reality General impressions Instances with dates, including your own contribution Gap count Three or four "areas" Exactly one, stated behaviourally Assignment An exercise created for development Work the business already needs, at a named delegation level Failure position Unstated Decided in advance and told to them Your own change Absent Specific, observable, and they may call you on it Checkpoints "We'll catch up" Dates in both calendars, plus a stated condition for rewriting the plan

A plan that scores "weak" on your own change is not a coaching plan. It is a performance-improvement document with friendlier typography, and the person will read it that way within a week.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Build the plan. Choose the person today, and run the two conversations inside two weeks — the first on the GROW worksheet from Module 1 to produce sections 1-3, the second to agree sections 4-8. Write it in the template in section 2, and give them the document; a coaching plan they have not read is a set of notes about someone.

Then apply the rubric in section 5 to your own plan honestly, and fix the two lowest-scoring rows before the first checkpoint. Pay particular attention to section 7: if you cannot name a specific behaviour of your own that has to change, you have almost certainly diagnosed a person where the real problem is a system you built.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Do the second one. Build a plan for the person you would have chosen last — the one whose potential you are least sure about. The "investigate" box in Module 8 is where the gap between your judgement and reality is widest.
  • Have them build yours. Ask your report to write the section 7 they would put in a coaching plan for you, and take it seriously. This is the sharpest available test of the psychological safety in Module 3.
  • Run the checkpoint as a coaching session, not a status update. At the 1 October equivalent, resist reviewing progress. Open with the Goal question again and see whether the goal has changed — if it has and it's still theirs, that's the plan working, not failing.
  • Coach a peer. Run a full GROW conversation with someone you have no authority over. Without positional power, leading questions stop working entirely, which is the fastest way to find out how much of your coaching was actually disguised advice.
  • Track the second-order effect. Six months on, ask whether the person you coached has started coaching someone else. That, rather than their own progress, is the measure of servant leadership at this level — and it is the entry condition for Level 3.
